title: Ericsson: 5G must shift focus from consumers to citizens, says UK chief
snippet: The future of 5G in the UK depends on recognising mobile networks as critical national infrastructure and moving beyond the narrow confines of consumer connectivity, according to Nadine Allen, Ericsson's Head of UK. The post Ericsson: 5G must shift focus from consumers to citizens, says UK chief appeared first on Total Telecom.
fullText:
Interview

The future of 5G in the UK depends on recognising mobile networks as critical national infrastructure and moving beyond the narrow confines of consumer connectivity, according to Nadine Allen, Ericsson’s Head of UK.

Speaking at Ericsson’s Elevate 5G event, Allen acknowledged the industry’s 5G revenue gap so far, arguing that 5G SA offers a major opportunity to revitalise 5G through the creation of new commercial models and the integration ofAI.

She called for a shift in perspective, moving away from what consumers want towards what citizens and critical services need.

“We need to shift away from a consumer focus to a citizen focus,” said Nadine. “That means anticipating not what users want from a network, but what they need from a network.”

The UK’s Emergency Services Network (ESN) is a perfect model for this type of collaboration between government and industry, wth Nadine suggesting similar approaches could benefit rail, energy, and defence.

“There are a number of industries that are either in the course of or due to go through quite significant transformation where I think the ESN model or similar can come into play,” said Nadine. “If we look at rail, for example, today on a 2G-based system, they’re moving to the Future Railway Mobile Communication System (FRMCS), which is based on 5G standards. We expect some commercial activity coming up in the foreseeable future for railways.”

The interview also touched on how AI is evolving in the UK and why robust wireless networks will be crucial to its ongoing growth and success.

“We are seeing AI move from data centres to distributed systems. And in order for those things to happen or to be brought to life in a meaningful way, we really have to ensure that we have very solid connectivity and underlying performance in networks,” said Nadine.

Watch the full interview to hear Nadine’s assessment of the UK’s 5G opportunity and what needs to happen next.

title: Africa’s Digital Progress Accelerates, but 64% Usage Gap Shows Next Challenge for Policymakers
snippet: GSMA Digital Africa Index 2026 finds seven more countries joining the continent’s leading group for digital development and enabling policy 18 November 2026, Cape Town: Africa is making measurable progress on digital development and enabling policy, but turning widespread mobile broadband coverage into meaningful digital participation remains a critical challenge, according to the GSMA’s flagship […] The post Africa’s Digital Progress Accelerates, but 64% Usage Gap Shows Next Challenge for Policymakers appeared first on Newsroom.
fullText:
GSMA Digital Africa Index 2026 finds seven more countries joining the continent’s leading group for digital development and enabling policy

18 November 2026, Cape Town: Africa is making measurable progress on digital development and enabling policy, but turning widespread mobile broadband coverage into meaningful digital participation remains a critical challenge, according to the GSMA’s flagship Digital Africa Index 2026, launched today at the GSMA Digital Africa Summit Cape Town.

Mobile broadband networks now cover 92% of Africa’s population, yet only 28% use mobile internet on their own devices, leaving a 64% usage gap. The cost of internet-enabled devices, limited digital skills and a lack of relevant local content and services remain significant barriers to adoption. While the usage gap is a global challenge, it is largest in Africa, making accelerating adoption across the region particularly urgent.

The Summit brings together policymakers, regulators and mobile industry leaders to address these challenges and explore how to extend the benefits of connectivity across Africa. Drawing on data from 54 countries, the Index gives delegates an evidence base to compare where reforms are driving progress and where further action is needed. This year’s report places particular focus on digital government and what it takes to turn the availability of online public services into meaningful use.

The Index also points to encouraging policy momentum. Ten African countries now combine stronger digital development with more enabling policy and regulation, up from three in 2024. Egypt, Ghana, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, Seychelles and Tunisia have joined Kenya, Mauritius and South Africa in the Index’s leading group.

Angela Wamola, Head of Africa, GSMA said: “Africa has made real progress in expanding mobile broadband coverage. The challenge now is ensuring that more people can actually use it. With 64% of the population living within coverage but not using mobile internet, closing the usage gap requires us to tackle the barriers that continue to keep people offline.

“South Africa shows what targeted reform can achieve. Making smartphones more affordable, building digital skills and ensuring people have access to relevant, trusted digital services can help turn connectivity into meaningful economic and social participation.”

Seven Countries Join the Index’s Leading Group

The Digital Africa Index draws on data from 54 African countries, assessing digital development alongside the policy and regulatory conditions that can enable it. This year’s report also focuses on digital government and what it takes to translate the availability of online public services into meaningful use.

Egypt, Ghana, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, Seychelles and Tunisia have joined Kenya, Mauritius and South Africa in the Index’s leading group for digital development and enabling policy and regulation.

South Africa and Kenya recorded the highest Digital Nations and Society Index (DNSI) scores, at 69 and 65 out of 100 respectively. Egypt and Ghana recorded the largest gains in their Digital Policy and Regulatory Index (DPRI) scores since 2024, supported by reforms across areas including cybersecurity, spectrum management, consumer protection and digital inclusion.

South Africa Shows the Impact of Smartphone Tax Reform

With mobile broadband already reaching most of Africa’s population, addressing the barriers preventing people from using the internet is increasingly important to unlocking the benefits of connectivity.

Device affordability is one of those barriers. Only nine of the 54 countries assessed impose neither sector-specific taxes nor import duties on mobile handsets, down from ten in 2024.

South Africa provides an example of how targeted tax reform can support smartphone adoption. After the country removed the 9% excise duty on smartphones priced below R2,500 in April 2025, monthly sales of entry-level smartphones increased by 80%, from around 250,000 in March 2025 to around 460,000 in February 2026, according to GSMA analysis.

The GSMA welcomes South Africa’s reform and urges governments in markets where import duties or sales taxes still apply to entry-level smartphones to remove those charges to help make getting online more affordable.

Alongside targeted tax reform, the report identifies sustainable device financing as another way to lower the upfront cost of internet-enabled devices. It also calls on regulators to make spectrum allocated to mobile services available at prices that support continued investment in coverage and network quality.

Digital Government: Moving from Access to Meaningful Use

The Digital Africa Index 2026 also examines how governments can ensure that putting public services online translates into better outcomes for people and businesses.

Simply making a service available digitally does not guarantee its use. People may still struggle to complete a transaction because of unreliable connectivity, language barriers or services that require users to complete part of the process in person.

The report identifies five areas where implementation can fall short: access; public value; trust and accountability; inclusion; and coordination across government agencies.

Five Priorities for Sustained and Inclusive Digital Use

To accelerate inclusive digital adoption, the GSMA identifies five priorities for governments, regulators and industry:

Make affordable and reliable connectivity a foundation of digital service delivery. Improve network quality, address the combined cost of devices and data, and design services that work on low-bandwidth connections.

Prioritise service completion and public value. Measure successful transactions, repeat use, user satisfaction and improvements in how services are delivered.

Strengthen trust and accountability. Enforce data protection, cybersecurity and consumer safeguards, supported by transparent oversight and clear mechanisms for people to raise complaints.

Build inclusion into digital service design. Expand accessible and local-language services, maintain assisted channels and address barriers facing rural, low-income and underserved communities.

Connect government systems securely. Improve coordination between agencies through shared digital identity, payment and data-exchange systems, with clear responsibilities for operating and securing them.

At the GSMA Digital Africa Summit Cape Town, the GSMA is encouraging governments, regulators, operators and development partners to use the Index’s country-level evidence to identify where coordinated action can accelerate progress, from lowering the cost of getting online to helping more people successfully access and complete essential services digitally.

-ENDS-

About GSMA

The GSMA is a global organisation unifying the mobile ecosystem to discover, develop and deliver innovation foundational to positive business environments and societal change. Our vision is to unlock the full power of connectivity so that people, industry, and society thrive. Representing mobile operators and organisations across the mobile ecosystem and adjacent industries, the GSMA delivers for its members across three broad pillars: Connectivity for Good, Industry Services and Solutions, and Outreach. This activity includes advancing policy, tackling today’s biggest societal challenges, underpinning the technology and interoperability that make mobile work, and providing the world’s largest platform to convene the mobile ecosystem at the MWC and M360 series of events.

title: Nokia, Telia and Nscale to lead AI Gigafactory Northern consortium
snippet: Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton Technologies, Telia and Verda have announced a new partnership to jointly develop federated AI infrastructure cross the Baltic and Nordic states. The post Nokia, Telia and Nscale to lead AI Gigafactory Northern consortium appeared first on Total Telecom.
fullText:
News

The project will see AI infrastructure deployed across Northern Europe

Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton Technologies, Telia and Verda have announced a new partnership to jointly develop federated AI infrastructure cross the Baltic and Nordic states.

The AI Gigafactory (AIGF) Northern consortium aims to deploy large-scale AI computing capacity with sovereign cloud services across multiple sites in multiple countries.

Initial sites include Oulu (Finland), Iru (Estonia,) and Valmiera (Latvia), with a Swedish location still to be confirmed.

These locations have been selected due to the reliable, decarbonised energy supply, availability advanced digital networks, and a cool climate that reduces cooling demand.

Nokia will provide connectivity infrastructure to link the sites and Nscale will provide its cloud platform and AI infrastructure knowledge. Telia, with its subsidiary Telia Cygate, will provide connectivity, data transmission, infrastructure operations and cloud solutions. Verda will provide AI-native expertise, particularly around training, and Skeleton will supply high-power systems to enhance data centre efficiency.

“Europe’s AI ambitions depend on infrastructure it can trust, control and scale. AIGF Northern brings together the connectivity, computing, cloud and energy capabilities needed to turn that ambition into reality,” said Mikko Hautala, Chief Geopolitical & Government Relations Officer, and Chairman at Nokia Defense. “By linking strengths across borders, we can build a more resilient foundation for European innovation, competitiveness and technological sovereignty.”

The project will also be supported by VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland, one of Europe’s leading research organisations, and KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Sweden’s largest technical university. Combined, these institutions will work alongside AIGF Northern members to align research, innovation, and talent networks.

Europe has been under pressure in recent years to rapidly scale its AI infrastructure capacity and reduce reliance on US technology. The EU’s InvestAI initiative aims to mobile €30 billion in investment to this end, combining €20 billion in private-sector funding with €10 billion from EU and national public sources.

AIGF Northern creates a partnership positioned to benefit from this funding, pledging to become a key player in Europe’s sovereign AI ecosystem.

“Our customers – and our continent – have a rapidly increasing need for scalable and trusted AI services. To meet this need, Europe’s best must step up,” said Anders Olsson, Executive Vice President, Head of Telia Sweden.
